claims.text: Reliable formation and superior catalytic performance of noble metal–based HEA nanomaterials rely on a uniformly mixed phase with atomic-level distribution of all constituent elements.
Rapid chemical reduction can maximize atomic mixing and minimize elemental segregation relative to slower thermal reduction.
A mild annealing step can improve crystallinity after rapid chemical reduction.
More uniform atomic mixing produces a higher density of uniform active sites.
A higher density of uniform active sites leads to more consistent and enhanced catalytic performance.
Fast nucleation limits the time available for elemental segregation.
Rapid reduction maximizes configurational mixing entropy.
Minimized segregation results in a homogeneous alloy with stable active surface sites.
Mild annealing can relieve residual strain and promote crystallinity without causing coarsening or phase separation.
Relieving strain and improving crystallinity stabilize the catalytic interface.
Rapidly reduced HEA nanomaterial will show a statistically significant improvement in catalytic turnover frequency relative to material produced by slower thermal reduction.
Rapidly reduced HEA nanomaterial will show a statistically significant improvement in reaction selectivity relative to material produced by slower thermal reduction.
Improved turnover frequency and selectivity are caused by a more uniform distribution of active sites and enhanced phase stability.
Slower thermal reduction typically produces a less uniform atomic distribution and potentially greater elemental segregation.
The proposed relationship is expected to hold for exclusively noble-metal HEA nanocatalysts at approximately 200–300°C and atmospheric pressure.
Annealing outside the appropriate kinetic window may trigger phase separation or grain coarsening.
The optimal reduction rate, annealing temperature, and annealing duration may vary with alloy composition.
